links.label: Purpose
links.context: The Agent Accountability Framework (AAF) helps your organization establish who each AI agent is, who answers for it, what it may do, and how to stop it. It turns those questions into requirements you can test. You choose how to meet them ([Purpose](source/01-purpose.md#1-purpose), [Implementation Neutrality](source/06-implementation-neutrality.md#6-implementation-neutrality)).

links.label: Section 2
links.context: The AAF covers agents acting in or on behalf of an organization with delegated authority to access information or take actions, including internal, external, and spawned agents. Controls are satisfied within the organization's own boundary. Model safety, general AI ethics, and the general operation and security of information systems are outside its scope ([Section 2](source/02-scope.md)).

links.label: Control 4.6
links.context: For example, if a document tricks an agent into trying an action outside its authority, that action must still be blocked. The framework constrains what the agent can do; it does not prescribe how to prevent the model from being manipulated ([Control 4.6](../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6)).

links.label: Control 1.4
links.context: Where a general practice has a consequence specific to agents, the framework makes that consequence a control and leaves the underlying practice to your organization. For example, within your organization's boundary, an agent may hold only its own identity credentials ([Control 1.4](../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-4)). How secrets are stored and distributed is outside the framework.

links.label: Control 3.8
links.context: You must still declare the agents, tools, models, and data sources an agent relies on and keep that dependency record current ([Control 3.8](../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-8)).

links.label: Section 4: Framework Core
links.context: This rule has normative effect: you must use it when applying every control ([Section 4: Framework Core](../source/04-framework-core.md#4-the-framework-core-principles-and-controls)). It follows the [Section 2 boundary rule](../source/02-scope.md#boundary-of-management).

links.label: Control 2.5
links.context: Where you cannot apply a control directly to that party, apply it to what crosses your boundary and to the relationship with the operator. Hold the operator to an agreement under [Control 2.5](../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5). The **operator of record** is the organization running the external agent, tool, or model, with an agreement assigning accountability and a named accountable contact.

- **Identity:** Identify the agent and manage the credentials it uses to act in your organization ([1.1](../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1), [1.3](../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)).

- **Identity:** Identify the agent and manage the credentials it uses to act in your organization ([1.1](../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1), [1.3](../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)).
- **Sponsor:** Name the internal human who answers for it ([2.1](../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)).
- **Role:** Define what it is admitted to do in your organization ([3.1](../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)).
- **Authority:** List the information it may access and the systems and tools it may use ([4.1](../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)).
- **Oversight:** Record what crosses your boundary ([5.1](../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1)).

- **Recourse:** Revoke its credentials, sessions, and authority at your boundary within the required suspension window. Work through its operator of record to pursue suspension of the runtime itself ([6.1](../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1), [2.5](../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)).

- **Recourse:** Revoke its credentials, sessions, and authority at your boundary within the required suspension window. Work through its operator of record to pursue suspension of the runtime itself ([6.1](../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1), [2.5](../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)).

If an agent you operate depends on an agent, tool, or model you do not control, declare that dependency ([3.8](../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-8)), bound the agent's access and outbound destinations ([4.1](../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1), [4.8](../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-8)), and hold the dependency to an operator of record ([2.5](../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)). links.label: Section 2 boundary rule
links.context: Every control is met from within your organization's own boundary. You do not need authority over another operator's people or systems. Where you cannot apply a control directly to an external agent, tool, or model, apply it to what crosses your boundary and to the relationship with its operator, and hold that operator to an agreement. This is the [Section 2 boundary rule](../source/02-scope.md#boundary-of-management).

links.label: Section 5: Conformance and Assessment
links.context: Source: [Section 5: Conformance and Assessment](../source/05-conformance-and-assessment.md#5-conformance-and-assessment).

links.label: Section 4
links.context: Section 5 explains what a conformance claim covers and what evidence you need. It gives guidance, rather than adding control requirements. It leaves the formal assessment method and conformance keywords undefined. Use each control's Requirement to decide whether it is met ([Section 4](../source/04-framework-core.md#4-the-framework-core-principles-and-controls)).

links.label: Scope tags and boundary rule
links.context: You can adopt the framework in stages by claiming a clearly stated subset of controls, provided that subset covers every agent in the estate. The [Scope tags and boundary rule](../source/04-framework-core.md#4-the-framework-core-principles-and-controls) still determine how each control applies.

links.label: Section 4
links.context: A finding against one agent is a finding against the estate, unless it is recorded as a declared exception with a remediation window. Record the exception and the time allowed to address it; an exception does not make a failed control pass. Each obligation in a control's Requirement must be met for that control to pass ([Section 4](../source/04-framework-core.md#4-the-framework-core-principles-and-controls)).

links.label: Control 3.3
links.context: Share confidence thresholds only with people who need to know them ([Control 3.3](../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-3)).

links.label: Control 6.1
links.context: Where the framework sets a minimum, your chosen parameter must meet it. For example, [Control 6.1](../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1) requires suspension in seconds. For an agent whose runtime you do not control, that means revoking its credentials, sessions, and authority at your boundary within the same window.

links.label: Section 4
links.context: The Requirement is the basis for deciding whether a control is met. Rationale explains why the requirement exists, and Assessment describes the evidence an assessor expects to see; both are guidance ([Section 4](../source/04-framework-core.md#4-the-framework-core-principles-and-controls)).

links.label: scope
links.context: An AAF conformance claim establishes agent accountability as the framework defines it. It does not establish that the organization is secure or that its models are safe or aligned. Those subjects remain outside the framework's [scope](../source/02-scope.md#2-scope).

links.label: Section 6: Implementation Neutrality
links.context: Source: [Section 6: Implementation Neutrality](../source/06-implementation-neutrality.md#6-implementation-neutrality).

links.label: Control 1.2
links.context: For example, a registry must provide an authoritative record of the agents admitted to act and the information required by [Control 1.2](../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2). You choose the technology that provides that record. The same principle applies to every control: choose the means, then show that the requirement is met.

links.label: Section 7: Relationship to Existing Standards
links.context: Source: [Section 7: Relationship to Existing Standards](../source/07-relationship-to-standards.md#7-relationship-to-existing-standards).

links.label: Section 5
links.context: These resources address different parts of the problem. Using one does not by itself establish AAF conformance; you still need evidence that your agents meet the controls you claim to meet ([Section 5](../source/05-conformance-and-assessment.md#5-conformance-and-assessment)).

links.label: Oversight
links.context: Section 7 also points to runtime governance practices in regulated industries that address the properties covered by [Oversight](../source/principles/05-oversight.md#principle-5-oversight) and [Recourse](../source/principles/06-recourse.md#principle-6-recourse).

links.label: Recourse
links.context: Section 7 also points to runtime governance practices in regulated industries that address the properties covered by [Oversight](../source/principles/05-oversight.md#principle-5-oversight) and [Recourse](../source/principles/06-recourse.md#principle-6-recourse).

links.label: Control 4.3
links.context: When an agent acts for someone else, the party receiving its request needs to verify who authorized it and what that authorization permits. Under [Control 4.3](../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3), the delegation must be explicit, attributable, bounded, and verifiable. The agent's effective authority cannot exceed either its own authority or the delegating principal's, and further delegation cannot add privileges.

links.label: Control 4.6
links.context: For example, an agent with permission to update customer records cannot use that permission on behalf of a person who may only read them. A document or tool response can carry a delegation, but the person or agent giving it must be authenticated and allowed to grant that authority, and the delegation must be recorded ([Control 4.6](../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6)).

The party holding defined authority to admit an agent to the registry and, separately, to production (control [1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)). Distinct from the sponsor; admission is a decision the sponsor does not make for their own agent.

links.label: Definition
links.context: Source: [Definition](../../source/appendices/a-terminology.md#agent).

A software actor powered wholly or partly by AI that holds delegated authority to access information or take actions on behalf of an organization. The unit of identity is one identity bound to a versioned configuration: the model, the harness, the instructions (system prompt, skills, rules, and seeded memory), and the tools and data sources the agent is given. A change to any element of the configuration is a change event ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4), [3.7](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-7)); a session or an instance of an agent is not a separate agent, and a different configuration under the same name is a different version of the agent.

The unique, durable identifier of an agent in the registry, distinct from every human user and every other agent ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)). One identity may be evidenced by several credentials over time and at once, and every credential resolves to exactly one identity. The identity, bound to a versioned configuration, is the unit to which every control attaches.

Autonomy is granted on measured reliability and reduced when reliability is not sustained.

links.label: Control 1.1
links.context: **Source:** [Control 1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1).

Every agent has a unique identity, distinct from every human user and every other agent, and authenticates with one or more verifiable credentials bound to that identity. A credential is bound to the single agent (its identity and its versioned configuration) it was issued to and is refused when presented by any other; an agent may hold several credentials over its lifetime and at one time, and each resolves to the same agent identity. No shared accounts, no anonymous execution, no agent operating under a human user’s credential, and no agent presenting another principal’s credential as its own. Where several agents share a runtime, the credential identifies the agent, not the runtime. When an agent acts on behalf of a human or another agent, the delegating principal and the acting agent remain independently identifiable ([4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3)). An agent does not create identities, accounts, or credentials for itself or for other agents in the organization’s systems outside the registry ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)); every identity and credential an agent needs is issued through the same lifecycle as its own ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)).

Accountability begins with attribution: every action must resolve to the agent that performed it, even when the agent shares a runtime, holds more than one credential, or acts on behalf of another principal. Identity and credential are distinct: the identity is the durable fact about the agent, and credentials are the evidence it presents, which rotate ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)) and multiply as the agent reaches different systems. Shared or borrowed credentials, impersonation, and delegated execution each obscure who actually acted, and make the remaining controls impossible to evaluate. A newer failure mode is the agent that opens an account for itself in a connected system: it has manufactured an identity the organization never issued, and every action under that account is unattributable by design.

For any observed action in any connected system, the assessor can resolve it to exactly one agent identity, regardless of the runtime or credential used. Where an agent holds several credentials, each resolves to the same identity in the registry. Where an agent acts on behalf of a human or another agent, both the delegating principal and the acting agent are independently attributable from the record ([5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1)). A sampled search finds no service accounts shared between agents and no agent authenticating as a human principal. A credential presented by an agent other than the identity it was issued to, or from a second workload, is refused at the enforcement point, and the event surfaces under control [5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2). A search of connected systems finds no account or identity created by an agent that is absent from the registry.

links.label: Control 1.2
links.context: **Source:** [Control 1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2).

Every agent admitted to act in or on behalf of the organization has a current record in an authoritative registry before it first acts, and no agent obtains access or invokes tools without a registry entry. The record binds the agent’s identity ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)) to its lifecycle state, its sponsor and owning team ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)), its approved configuration and version, and its permitted runtime context. Enrollment is an approval by a party holding defined authority (the admitting authority) to admit an agent to the registry and, separately, to admit it to production; an agent does not enroll itself, and the admitting authority is not the agent’s sponsor. Admission may be granted to a template: an agent instantiated from an approved template with no change to its configuration is admitted on instantiation and recorded individually, so that short-lived spawned agents are admitted at machine speed without the approval becoming a formality. For each agent the organization operates, the registry also records the harness that runs it and the harness settings that bear on its accountability (iteration limits, memory, whether it may create spawned agents, available tools and models), the runtime locations in which it is permitted to execute, and its agent class attributes: model, agent type, and workload label. For an external agent, the registry records its operator of record ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)) and the role of its engagement ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)). The tools and models an agent is authorized to invoke are registered under control [4.13](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-13), and the registry population is reconciled against observation under control [5.8](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-8).

links.label: Control 1.3
links.context: **Source:** [Control 1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3).

Agent identity credentials are issued, rotated, and revoked through a managed lifecycle. Credentials are short-lived or attestation-based by default; static long-lived secrets are not used as agent identity. A credential is accepted only by the resource it was issued for and only from the identity it was issued to; a credential that is valid everywhere, or usable by whoever holds it, is not an agent identity credential. For an external agent, this control applies to the credential it uses to act in the organization. Where a third-party service cannot enforce audience or holder binding on the credentials it accepts, the organization brokers the access ([1.4](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-4)) so that the credential never leaves the enforcement layer.

links.label: Control 1.4
links.context: **Source:** [Control 1.4](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-4).

Within the organization’s boundary, an agent is given no credential other than its own identity credential ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)). Access to the organization’s systems, tools, and models, and to third-party services the organization brokers, is provided to the agent at the moment of use by the enforcement layer, from a managed store, and is mediated at the point of use: the credential is exchanged, narrowed, or translated to the audience and scope the action requires ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)), and it is never placed in the agent’s prompt, context, configuration, memory, or code. A credential an agent encounters in the course of its work, whether in a file, a repository, a web page, a tool response, or a message from another agent, is unusable in the organization by design. An attempt to use one is recorded and escalated ([6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3)); the first response is scoped to the agent that made the attempt, and estate-wide revocation ([6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1)) follows only on corroboration that the credential is valid and in use beyond that agent, so that planted credentials cannot be used to force a shutdown.

Within the organization’s boundary, an agent is given no credential other than its own identity credential ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)). Access to the organization’s systems, tools, and models, and to third-party services the organization brokers, is provided to the agent at the moment of use by the enforcement layer, from a managed store, and is mediated at the point of use: the credential is exchanged, narrowed, or translated to the audience and scope the action requires ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)), and it is never placed in the agent’s prompt, context, configuration, memory, or code. A staged exercise in which a canary credential (one the agent would treat as valid but which confers nothing) is placed within the agent’s reach results in refusal when the agent attempts to use it, and the attempt is recorded under control [5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1) and escalated under control [6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3) with the first response scoped to that agent.

links.label: Control 1.5
links.context: **Source:** [Control 1.5](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-5).

Every action an agent takes that is material to its role, including tool invocations, API calls, and messages to other agents, carries verifiable evidence of its origin and integrity: which agent produced it, under which delegation ([4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3)), and that it was not altered in transit. A party relied upon to act on an agent’s request can verify that evidence without trusting the agent’s own assertion, and declines a request whose provenance cannot be established. This control governs actions on the organization’s systems and between its agents; where an external receiver cannot verify provenance, the organization’s enforcement layer verifies it before the action leaves the boundary.

Attribution ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)) establishes that an agent has an identity; provenance establishes that a given action was really its. Without it, a message that claims to come from a registered agent is indistinguishable from one injected by an attacker or fabricated by another agent, and the audit record ([5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1)) is a record of claims rather than of facts. The framework requires that provenance be verifiable; it does not prescribe the signing or attestation mechanism, which is an area of active standards work ([Section 7](../../source/07-relationship-to-standards.md)).

Every agent maps at all times to exactly one accountable human sponsor and to an owning team, both recorded in the registry ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)). The sponsor is a named individual, not a team, a role title, or a service account. Ownership is also recorded for each agent class (the agents sharing a model, an agent type, a harness, or a workload label), so that when a whole class must be halted ([6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1)) there is a named person accountable for the decision and its consequences. This includes every external agent admitted to act in the organization: its sponsor is the internal person who answers for its admission ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)), for its role in the organization ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)), and for the authority granted to it ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)). The operator of record ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)) does not replace the internal sponsor. The sponsor has acknowledged the sponsorship, the consequence of answering for an agent is defined by the organization in its own management processes and known to the sponsor, and the organization declares a limit on the number of agents a sponsor may hold, counted including spawned agents; a sponsor at the limit is assigned no more.

Accountability terminates in a person, not a system. A team can operate an agent, but a team cannot answer for it in the way a person can; diffuse ownership is functionally no ownership. Recording the owning team alongside the sponsor places the agent inside the organization's existing structures for budget, review, and security instead of leaving it a personal project. Class-level ownership exists because some failures arrive by class: a model that changes behavior, a harness with a vulnerability, a workload type that turns out to have been misconfigured. Halting every agent of that class is a decision someone must own. For an external agent, the internal sponsor is who the organization holds accountable, and the operator of record ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)) is who the sponsor reaches when recourse must extend beyond the boundary.

A change to the sponsor or the owning team, including departure, transfer, or role change, triggers automatic reassignment or decommissioning within a defined window. Reassignment takes effect on the new sponsor’s recorded acknowledgement; until then the agent is held by a named member of the escalation set ([6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3)), and an agent not acknowledged within the window is suspended ([6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1)). No agent is unsponsored at any point in its lifecycle, and this applies equally to the internal sponsor of an external agent.

An agent created by another agent is sponsored by its parent’s sponsor from the moment it exists, and the sponsor’s accountability for it is the same as for the parent. The parent agent is recorded as the delegating principal ([4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3)) and may be the accountable party for the spawned agent’s conduct within the organization’s management structure, but accountability still terminates in the sponsor. A spawned agent is identified ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)), enrolled ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)), and governed under every principle; it is not an extension of its parent’s session. An agent is created inside the organization only through the organization’s own admission ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)) and only by a parent whose authority permits it ([4.14](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-14)). An external agent cannot create an agent inside the organization except through that admission; an agent so admitted is operated by the organization, sponsored by the external parent’s internal sponsor ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)), and holds at most the authority its parent holds in the organization. An agent spawned outside the boundary is an external agent when it acts in the organization.

A spawned agent is identified ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)), enrolled ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)), and governed under every principle; it is not an extension of its parent’s session. An agent is created inside the organization only through the organization’s own admission ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)) and only by a parent whose authority permits it ([4.14](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-14)). An external agent cannot create an agent inside the organization except through that admission; an agent so admitted is operated by the organization, sponsored by the external parent’s internal sponsor ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)), and holds at most the authority its parent holds in the organization. An agent spawned outside the boundary is an external agent when it acts in the organization.

For a sampled spawned agent, the registry shows its sponsor as its parent’s sponsor and its parent as its delegating principal, and the record under control [5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1) reconstructs the chain from the spawned agent to the sponsor. No agent in the estate whose creator is an agent lacks a sponsor of record.

links.label: Control 2.5
links.context: **Source:** [Control 2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5).

Every external agent admitted to act in the organization, and every external tool or model on which an agent the organization operates depends, maps to a verified operating organization, an agreement that assigns accountability for its conduct and for the controls the organization cannot apply from within its own boundary, and a named accountable contact at the operator. The operator of record is the second line of accountability: the internal sponsor ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)) answers for admission, role, and authority inside the organization, and relies on the operator of record for recourse that must reach beyond the boundary.

The organization cannot run an agent it does not operate, and it cannot apply this framework inside a vendor. What it can do is name the person inside who answers for the engagement ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)), and hold the organization that operates the agent to an agreement with a named person on the other end of it. Without an operator of record, recourse stops at the credential the organization can revoke. Where an operator of record cannot be obtained on the operator’s terms, as for a commodity model or tool, the internal sponsor records acceptance of the gap together with the compensating controls applied at the boundary ([1.4](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-4), [3.8](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-8), [4.8](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-8), [4.11](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-11)), and the dependency is recorded as accepted rather than ungoverned. The operator’s identity and reachability are verified before admission and re-verified on a defined cadence; an operator that cannot be reached is a change event for every agent and dependency it operates.

links.label: Control 3.1
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1).

Every agent has a documented, scoped purpose: expected outcomes and explicit out-of-scope boundaries. The role is expressed as rules and intents. A rule is deterministic: an action satisfies it or does not. An intent is not, and is declared with the measure by which it is evaluated, a confidence score produced under Oversight ([5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6)), and the confidence thresholds at which defined levels of recourse apply ([6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3)). The role also declares its reach: the systems, data domains, and external parties the agent can affect. The documented role is the authoritative source from which enforced policy ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1), [4.2](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-2)) is derived, and it is held in a form that cannot be altered without detection. For an external agent, the role is the role of the engagement: what the agent is admitted to do in the organization, defined by the organization.

links.label: Section 4
links.context: Neither authority nor deviation can be evaluated without a reference point. The out-of-scope boundary matters as much as the purpose itself, because an agent doing something useful but unmandated is still a governance failure. Not everything a role requires can be written as a pass or fail. An agent that serves the requests of the people who use it, or that exercises judgment within a purpose, is governed by intents, and an intent is only a control when the role says how it will be measured and what happens at each level of confidence. Declaring the thresholds in the role makes recourse a consequence of the job description rather than a decision improvised at runtime. Declaring reach gives the organization the measure by which it scales oversight ([Section 4](../../source/04-framework-core.md)). Making the role tamper-evident keeps it a control: a role that can be quietly edited is a role that can be quietly widened.

The role description exists, is versioned, and states both expected outcomes and explicit exclusions. From the document alone, an assessor can name at least one action the agent is capable of but not mandated to perform. The role distinguishes its rules from its intents; every intent names its measure and the confidence thresholds that trigger each level of recourse; the role names its reach; and a staged alteration of the role outside the change process ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4)) is detectable.

links.label: Control 3.2
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.2](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-2).

Every active agent has defined, measurable success criteria. The criteria include whether the agent is used and whether it returns value against its purpose and its budget ([3.5](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-5)), not only whether it behaves; value is assessed against the criteria the sponsor declared, not against the assessor’s judgment of worth.

“Is this agent performing well?” is answerable in objective terms at any point in its lifecycle, by a party outside the deploying team, from the recorded criteria and current measurements. The recorded criteria include measures of utilization and value, and the current measurements under control [5.5](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-5) report against them.

links.label: Control 3.3
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.3](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-3).

The role is documented to the standard of a job description: a party outside the deploying team, whether auditor, security, or leadership, can determine from it what the agent should and should not be doing. The confidence thresholds declared under [3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1) and [4.7](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-7) are held with the role but disclosed only to parties with a need to know; readability beyond the team does not make the thresholds public.

links.label: Control 3.4
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4).

The documented role reflects the agent’s actual current use. When scope changes, the role is re-scoped, and authority re-derived, before or with the change rather than after it. Every version of the role is retained, and a change to the role is a change event: it is proposed, approved by a party with authority over the role, applied as a new version, and followed by re-derivation of the agent’s authority ([4.2](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-2)) and re-validation of its behavior against the new version ([5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6)) before the agent acts under it. Changes are tiered by their effect on the role, its intents, its reach, and the authority derived from it: a change below a declared threshold follows a lighter path, and a change that widens the role, its intents, or its reach above a declared reach threshold is approved by a second party other than the sponsor and treated as a new admission to production ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)).

links.label: Control 3.5
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.5](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-5).

Every role declares a budget bound: the tokens, spend, or other resource units the agent may consume over a defined period, and per run where a single run can be material. The bound is enforced at the enforcement layer as a cap, consumption is metered and attributed to the agent and its sponsor ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)), and consumption is measured against the bound under control [5.5](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-5). The bound includes limits on concurrency, enforced at the enforcement layer for every agent, and on iteration, enforced in the harness and reported to the enforcement layer for agents the organization operates, so that a runaway loop or an uncontrolled fan-out of work is stopped as a budget breach. Where an agent delegates work to other agents or creates spawned agents ([4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3), [4.14](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-14)), the budget of the delegated task is a single bound on the aggregate consumption of every agent working on it, counted across the whole tree and reserved at the point of approval, so that neither the division of the task nor the timing of separate checks can approve in parts what the bound would deny as a whole.

links.label: Control 3.6
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.6](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-6).

Every role declares its autonomy level: the degree to which the agent may act without a human disposition, expressed as the consequence threshold applied under control [5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3) and the action classes the agent may execute below it. The level is granted only after the agent has met its success criteria ([3.2](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-2)) over a defined period and has withstood adversarial testing ([5.7](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-7)) at that level, since reliability on benign inputs is not evidence of robustness, and is reduced, with the threshold adjusted accordingly, when the agent fails either.

links.label: Control 3.7
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.7](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-7).

Every role declares the model or models the agent uses and the harness that runs it, as registered ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)). A change to either, including a change made by a model or harness provider beneath an unchanged name or version label, is a change event ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4)): the agent is re-validated against its role ([5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6)) before it acts under the new model or harness, and its authority is re-derived where the change affects what it can do. The role also binds the agent’s live instructions: its system prompt, skills, rules, and seeded memory. The instructions running at any moment match the approved version of the role; a change to them is a change event ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4)), and a mismatch between the running instructions and the approved version is a deviation ([5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2)). Because a provider may change a model behind an unchanged label, the organization detects such change by behavioral sampling against the baseline ([5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2)), and this control is satisfied when the sampling runs on the defined cadence and a detected change triggers re-validation. A change made to remediate a disclosed vulnerability may proceed under an emergency exception: the agent operates at reduced autonomy ([3.6](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-6)) until re-validation completes within a defined time.

links.label: Control 3.8
links.context: **Source:** [Control 3.8](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-8).

Every role declares the agents, tools, models, and data sources the agent depends on to perform its role, and the registry ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)) derives from those declarations which agents depend on this one. Dependencies are declared before the agent acts and are kept current under control [3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4). An agent may discover tools at runtime only within a set or agent class recorded in the registry ([4.13](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-13)); a discovered tool outside it is unregistered. Before any dependency is changed, suspended, or decommissioned, its dependents are identified and a disposition for each is recorded ([6.5](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-5)). For a dependency the organization does not operate, the role also declares the agent’s disposition when that dependency changes or becomes unavailable: continue, degrade, hold, or stop.

links.label: Control 4.1
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1).

An agent’s authority is enumerated across both dimensions: the data and information it can access, and the systems and tools it can invoke. “What can this agent see, and what can this agent do?” is answerable from the record, completely. The data dimension is expressed against the organization’s data classification, so that what an agent can see is stated in named classes of data and not only in named systems. A general-purpose tool (a shell, a browser, a query interface, code execution) is enumerated by the reach it is permitted, not by the tool’s name: the resources, destinations, and data domains it may affect, enforced under [4.4](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-4) and [4.8](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-8).

links.label: Control 4.2
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.2](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-2).

Every grant in the enumeration traces back to a named element of the documented role: a declared outcome, a rule, or an intent ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)), or an action class the role permits. A grant that has not been exercised over a declared period is reviewed and either re-justified against the role or revoked ([4.5](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-5)); the period is declared in the role and is no longer than the role’s review cadence.

Every grant in the enumeration traces back to a named element of the documented role: a declared outcome, a rule, or an intent ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)), or an action class the role permits. A grant that has not been exercised over a declared period is reviewed and either re-justified against the role or revoked ([4.5](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-5)); the period is declared in the role and is no longer than the role’s review cadence.

This makes least privilege testable. Instead of asking whether any grant is dangerous, the assessor asks whether every grant is justified, and that question has an answer. Tracing each grant to a named element of the role, rather than to a task the reader must infer, is what lets a party outside the deploying team ([3.3](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-3)) check the trace. A grant that is justified but never used is authority waiting for a misuse; the review converts dormancy into a decision.

links.label: Control 4.3
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3).

When an agent acts on behalf of a human, or of another agent, the delegated authority is explicitly recorded, bound to the delegator’s identity, and never exceeds the authority the delegator holds. Delegation may be standing or dynamic, conferred in the course of operations by a principal authorized to confer it; in either case it is attributable, bounded, and verifiable by any party relied upon to act on it. An agent cannot extend its own authority by inference, and delegation chains cannot amplify privilege at any hop. For delegation involving an external agent ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)), the delegation identifies both the authorizing principal and the acting agent. An agent acting on behalf of a principal is limited to the intersection of its own authority and the principal’s, so that a broad agent cannot do for a narrow user what the user could not do. Authority conferred on a spawned agent is a delegation under this control and is further bounded under control [4.14](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-14).

Authority conferred on a spawned agent is a delegation under this control and is further bounded under control [4.14](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-14).

Delegation is how authority actually moves in agentic systems, and how it leaks. Without a binding to the delegator, “on behalf of” becomes a laundering mechanism: an agent accumulates permissions no single principal ever held. The no-amplification rule keeps multi-agent chains governable, because each hop can only narrow. Verifiability completes the loop: the party receiving a delegated request must be able to confirm the agent’s identity ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1), [1.5](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-5)) and the delegation it claims without trusting the agent’s own assertion, and for requests above a consequence threshold, confirmation with the delegator is an available disposition ([5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3)). The framework requires that delegation be explicit and verifiable; it does not prescribe the mechanism, which is an active area of standards work ([Section 7](../../source/07-relationship-to-standards.md)).

links.label: Control 4.4
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.4](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-4).

Authorization is issued and enforced by the same system of record. There is no gap where an agent holds credentials, data access, or tool entitlements the enforcement layer does not know about. Every path by which an agent reaches a governed resource passes through the enforcement point that applies the resource’s policy, including paths through composite tools and workflows that call the resource on the agent’s behalf. A direct path that bypasses enforcement is closed, not merely prohibited. Where a path exists inside a vendor’s product that the organization cannot close, it is recorded as a boundary gap and compensated under [2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5) and [4.8](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-8). The organization declares the degraded mode of the enforcement layer when it is unavailable; bypassing the enforcement layer is never a degraded mode.

The organization declares the degraded mode of the enforcement layer when it is unavailable; bypassing the enforcement layer is never a degraded mode.

A grant the enforcement layer cannot see is a grant that cannot be revoked, audited, or minimized. When authorization is issued in one place, enforced in another, and never reconciled, enumerated authority ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) quietly diverges from actual authority. A single system of record is defeated by a second door. Composite tools are the common one: a workflow tool that calls three systems is three grants wearing one name, and if its calls are not enforced per resource, the enumeration ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) is wrong.

links.label: Section 5
links.context: Authority is revocable in real time across both dimensions, and every grant carries an explicit validity bound. Authority expires by default rather than persisting by default. The real-time window is declared by the organization ([Section 5](../../source/05-conformance-and-assessment.md)) and is no longer than the shortest credential lifetime and cache period in use downstream.

links.label: Control 4.6
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.6](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6).

An agent’s authority derives exclusively from explicit grant and delegation ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)–[4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3)). A delegation is distinguished from ordinary content by the authenticated identity and authority of the delegator and by its capture in the record. Content that is not an authenticated delegation, whether documents, messages, tool outputs, web pages, or the outputs of other agents, confers no authority. An action motivated by such content is evaluated against the agent’s granted and delegated authority, undiminished and unexpanded.

links.label: Section 2
links.context: The distinction is between an instruction from a principal that is known and entitled to give it and an instruction from a source that is neither, however plausibly worded. Injected instructions are an attempted delegation by an unauthenticated principal. The framework does not prescribe how manipulation of an agent is prevented; model behavior is out of scope ([Section 2](../../source/02-scope.md)). It requires instead that a successfully manipulated agent still cannot act beyond what was legitimately granted or delegated. The blast radius of a compromised agent is its enumeration, never more. Enforcement rests on the action and the authenticated delegation, never on parsing the instruction: the framework does not assume an agent can tell a delegator’s words from untrusted material carried in the same channel, and an assessor does not test whether it can.

Enforcement of authority is demonstrated to be independent of the agent’s own reasoning: the agent arguing for an action does not change what it is permitted to do. An exercise in which unauthenticated content instructs the agent to exceed its authority results in denial at the enforcement layer and surfaces under control [5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2). An equivalent instruction delivered as an authenticated delegation from an authorized principal is honored within the delegator’s bounds and recorded under control [4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3).

links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.7](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-7).

Authority is expressed as rules and intents ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)). A request is evaluated against both. A rule it fails is denied. An intent produces a confidence score that the request serves the purpose the authority declares, and the confidence thresholds declared with that intent determine whether the request proceeds, proceeds with restriction, is held for human decision, or is denied, as the levels of recourse are defined under control [6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3). The evaluation is made at the point of entry, before the request reaches the model, and again at the point of action, before the agent affects any governed resource, and every result below a threshold is recorded ([5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1)). Intent evaluation covers the trajectory of an agent’s actions as well as each request ([5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6)), so that a sequence of individually acceptable requests is scored as a whole. When the evaluator or the enforcement layer is unavailable, actions above the pre-execution threshold ([5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3)) fail closed, and the organization declares the behavior for actions below it. For an agent the organization operates, the point of entry is before the request reaches the model. Intents are declared where a purpose cannot be expressed as rules; an authority whose purpose is fully expressed as rules declares no intents and is evaluated against rules alone, and the role records that determination ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)). The evaluator that produces the confidence score is subject to control [5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6): it is validated, independent of the content it scores, and re-validated with each change event.

links.label: Control 4.8
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.8](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-8).

Every agent has an explicit set of permitted outbound destinations, derived from its role ([4.2](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-2)), and all other destinations are denied by default at the enforcement layer. Destinations whose primary use is relaying or storing data outside the organization’s control are denied unless the role specifically requires them. An agent cannot cause the enforcement layer, or any system it reaches, to fetch from or send to a destination on its behalf that it could not reach directly. A tool that sends (mail, tickets, shared documents, webhooks) is itself a destination: its recipients are bounded under this control, and sending through it to an unlisted recipient is denied.

Where an agent can send is part of what it can do, and it is the part through which data leaves. An agent that can reach an arbitrary endpoint can exfiltrate anything it can read, and the incidents that have already occurred used exactly the destinations this control denies by default: paste services, tunnels, webhooks, hosted spaces. Default-deny egress bounds the damage a compromised or misdirected agent can do to what it can reach, which is the enumeration ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) and nothing more.

For sampled agents, the permitted destinations are produced from the record and trace to the role. A staged request to an unlisted destination, directly or through a system the agent can instruct, is denied at the enforcement layer and surfaces under control [5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2).

links.label: Control 4.9
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.9](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-9).

Every agent that executes code, generates or causes code to run, or acts on the host it runs on, and any code it generates or causes to run, executes within a containment boundary that limits what it can reach to its enumerated authority ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)). The boundary prevents access to the services of the host it runs on, limits filesystem access to the agent’s own working space and to remote resources it is explicitly authorized to use, and ensures that anything the agent runs inside the boundary is attributable to the agent ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)) and subject to the same enforcement. The boundary isolates the agent’s execution from the host and from other agents at the level of the operating system kernel or stronger; isolation only at the level of a process or a namespace does not meet this control. An agent with no such capability satisfies this control by having none: its registered configuration ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)) and its enumeration ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) show no code execution and no local effect, and a staged attempt to execute code is refused.

links.label: Control 4.10
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.10](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-10).

An agent’s retrieved context, working memory, and persistent memory are isolated per agent and, where the agent serves multiple principals, per principal. No agent reads or writes another agent’s memory or context except through a governed interface in its enumeration ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)), and no shared writable resource exists across agent instances or runs unless it is itself behind the enforcement layer with per-identity write isolation.

Memory is where an agent’s instructions come from tomorrow. A memory one agent can poison is an instruction channel into another, and context that leaks across principals is a data breach that happens inside the agent rather than at its edge. Isolation keeps the content an agent processes ([4.6](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6)) its own, so that what it has been told cannot be rewritten by a party that was never authorized to tell it anything.

links.label: Control 4.11
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.11](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-11).

The data boundary of the role ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) is enforced in both directions at the point of action. Before data leaves the organization’s control, including in prompts or context sent to a model the organization does not operate and in responses or messages sent to an external party or external agent, content outside the agent’s data authority is removed, masked, or tokenized. Before an agent acts on data it receives, the data is checked against the agent’s data authority and held or denied where it exceeds it. The clause on prompts and context applies to agents the organization operates. The organization declares the tolerance of the masking it applies, and masking that would defeat the task results in a held action under [5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3) rather than a silent failure.

An agent’s data authority is meaningless if the data can leave in a prompt or arrive in a response. Models the organization does not operate, and agents it does not sponsor, are outside the boundary, and what crosses to them is a disclosure. Enforcing the boundary at the point of action, rather than relying on the agent to observe it, is the same principle as control [4.6](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6): the agent’s judgment is not the control.

A staged prompt or outbound message containing data outside the agent’s authority is masked or held at the enforcement layer before it leaves, and a staged inbound payload exceeding the agent’s data authority is held or denied. The record under control [5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1) shows the intervention.

links.label: Control 4.12
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.12](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-12).

An agent’s role and authority are designed so that, within a single session, the agent does not combine all three of the following: processing content from sources the organization does not control, holding access to sensitive systems or data, and the ability to change state or communicate outside the organization. Where a role requires all three, the combination is declared in the role, the actions that complete it are rated above the pre-execution threshold ([5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3)), and the design is approved as part of admission to production ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)). The combination is evaluated across the agent graph and persistent memory, not only within one session: where agents that exchange messages or share memory jointly hold all three conditions, the combination is declared, rated, and approved in the same way, with a named sponsor for the combination. Untrusted content is defined in [Appendix A](../../source/appendices/a-terminology.md).

links.label: Appendix A
links.context: An agent’s role and authority are designed so that, within a single session, the agent does not combine all three of the following: processing content from sources the organization does not control, holding access to sensitive systems or data, and the ability to change state or communicate outside the organization. The combination is evaluated across the agent graph and persistent memory, not only within one session: where agents that exchange messages or share memory jointly hold all three conditions, the combination is declared, rated, and approved in the same way, with a named sponsor for the combination. Untrusted content is defined in [Appendix A](../../source/appendices/a-terminology.md).

The three conditions together are the anatomy of nearly every agent compromise: untrusted content carries an instruction, access makes it possible, and an outbound capability makes it consequential. Removing any one of the three makes a successful manipulation ([4.6](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6)) survivable. The framework does not forbid the combination, because some roles need it; it requires that it be a decision rather than a default.

For every role in the estate, and for every set of agents connected by messages or shared memory, the assessor can state which of the three conditions it holds. Roles holding all three are declared as such, their completing actions appear above the [5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3) threshold, and their admission record shows the combination was approved.

links.label: Control 4.13
links.context: **Source:** [Control 4.13](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-13).

Every tool and every model an agent is authorized to invoke is registered, with the authorized definition of each held in the registry ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)): for a tool, its name, description, and input schema, or a pinned version or hash of them; for a model, its provider, identifier, and version. Invocation is checked against the registered definition at the enforcement layer ([4.4](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-4)), and a tool or model whose definition differs from the one registered is treated as unregistered until it is re-approved. A registered tool whose observed behavior departs from its registered definition is treated as changed ([5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2)) even where its name and schema have not. A grant in an agent’s enumeration ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) refers to a registered definition, never to a name alone. An agent may discover tools at runtime only within a set recorded in the registry ([3.8](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-8)); a discovered tool outside it is unregistered.

Every tool and every model an agent is authorized to invoke is registered, with the authorized definition of each held in the registry ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)): for a tool, its name, description, and input schema, or a pinned version or hash of them; for a model, its provider, identifier, and version. Invocation is checked against the registered definition at the enforcement layer ([4.4](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-4)), and a tool or model whose definition differs from the one registered is treated as unregistered until it is re-approved. A framework that governs only known tools is defeated by a tool whose definition changes after it was authorized. A tool that keeps its name and its grant while its behavior changes is authority granted to something the organization never reviewed, and a model swapped beneath a stable label is the same failure in a different place ([3.7](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-7)). Registering the definition, and enforcing against it, is what makes an enumeration of authority ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) an enumeration of things rather than of names.

When an agent creates a spawned agent ([2.4](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-4)), the spawned agent holds its own identity ([1.1](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-1)) and its own authority, conferred by the parent as a delegation ([4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3)): at most a subset of the parent’s authority, never all of it by default, and never the parent’s identity or credential. The union of the authority held by all agents spawned from one parent cannot exceed the parent’s authority, and the bound applies to the aggregate at any moment, not only hop by hop. Spawning is delegation in a new form, and it compounds: if each agent may create three agents with its own authority, the third generation is twenty-seven agents with the authority of the first. Spawning differs from delegation between existing agents in that the parent creates the actor as well as conferring the authority, which is why the spawned agent is an agent in its own right ([2.4](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-4)) rather than an extension of its parent acting under the parent’s identity. Bounding the tree as a whole, rather than each parent, is what prevents a swarm from assembling inside the rules.

A sampled spawned agent holds its own identity and less authority than its parent, and the aggregate authority of a sampled set of siblings is within the parent’s. A staged attempt to spawn beyond the declared depth or tree size is refused at the enforcement layer. A staged attempt by an external agent to instantiate an agent inside the organization without admission ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)) is refused.

links.context: **Source:** [Control 5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1).

Every action produces a tamper-evident record in two parts. The evidence part is kept for every action: what, when, the triggering context, the full delegation chain, the action’s provenance ([1.5](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-5)), any disposition applied ([5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3)), the source of the content that influenced the action, so that the record can name the author of an instruction and not only the agent that acted on it, and a tamper-evident reference to each item of content involved. When agents invoke agents, the evidence part reconstructs the complete chain of authority back to the accountable human sponsor, not just the immediate actor. The content part holds everything that crosses the organization’s boundary for the action and, for an agent the organization operates, the inputs the agent acted on (prompts, retrieved context, and tool responses) and the model’s outputs; it is reachable from the evidence part by reference, is classified and retained under the organization’s records and data classification obligations, and may be masked or tokenized under control [4.11](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-11) where the classification requires it. Tamper evidence holds for both parts against the agent, its sponsor, its owning team, and the administrators of the systems the agent uses; the organization declares whether administrators of the record itself are within the threat model. Retention and erasure duties are reconciled in a declared policy, and content stored in the record is treated as untrusted input ([4.6](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6)) by any person or tool that reads it.

Accountability is reconstructable history. A record the agent or its owner can amend is testimony, not evidence, and a record that names only the last hop hides the principal. The chain-to-sponsor requirement is what makes multi-agent systems answerable to a person ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)). What the agent was told and what the model said are the evidence that explains an action; an action without them can be attributed but not understood. Separating evidence from content lets the organization keep the proof of who acted, and under what authority, for as long as accountability requires, while handling prompts and context, which are large and often sensitive, under the rules that already govern such data.

Deviations from the documented role ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)) or enumerated authority ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)) surface while the agent is running, generating an alert to a party with the authority to act, or a real-time system-based restriction or constraint, not only in post-incident review. Deviation includes a confidence score against an intent declared in the role or authority ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1), [4.7](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-7)) falling below its declared threshold, and change in the agent’s behavior under an unchanged role and unchanged inputs, which indicates a change in the model or harness beneath it ([3.7](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-7)). Deviation is evaluated against a recorded baseline of expected behavior for the role. The baseline is a statistical description with a declared tolerance, since model output varies run to run, and deviation is a departure beyond the tolerance. The baseline is established from behavior observed under evaluation ([5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6)), not from unreviewed production behavior; it is re-established with each change event ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4)), with the re-establishment reviewed, and on a defined cadence, so that slow change in retrieval sources or tool backends is caught without a change event. The party alerted has the declared capacity to act within the window: coverage and triage are declared, not assumed.

links.context: **Source:** [Control 5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3).

Action classes are rated by consequence, considering at minimum reversibility, materiality, and external impact. Classes above a defined threshold, the threshold for each agent being the one set by its autonomy level ([3.6](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-6)), are evaluated before execution, with a defined disposition for every proposed action: proceed, proceed with flag, hold for human decision, or deny. Prior approval does not carry forward; disposition attaches to each action, not to the session. Action classes include sequences: a sequence of actions whose combined consequence exceeds the threshold is rated as a class. The evidence presented to a human decider is produced by the enforcement layer from the proposed action itself (the action, its parameters, the resources affected, and the agent’s role and authority), not composed by the agent; text the agent wrote may accompany it, marked as such. The decider has a declared minimum time, and the volume of held actions per decider is bounded so that disposition remains a decision.

The consequence rating scheme and threshold are documented and applied to every action class in the enumeration ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1)). For sampled high-consequence actions, the record shows disposition preceding execution, and held actions show the deciding human, the decision, and its timestamp. No standing session-level approval covers individual high-consequence actions.

links.label: Control 5.4

The audit trail is queryable by parties outside the agent’s owning team. Access is bounded by need to know, is itself recorded, and treats the content it returns as untrusted input ([5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1)).

links.label: Control 5.6
links.context: **Source:** [Control 5.6](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-6).

Every agent is evaluated against its role before it enters production, before it acts under any change event ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4), [3.7](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-7)), and continuously while it operates. Evaluation covers conformance to role, authority, and intent, resistance to manipulation through content ([4.6](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-6)), and the agent’s success criteria ([3.2](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-2)). Evaluations follow the two kinds of definition in the role and authority ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1), [4.7](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-7)): rules, which an action passes or fails, and intents, for which the evaluation produces the confidence score the intent declares as its measure, compared against the confidence thresholds declared with it, at which the result becomes a disposition under control [5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3) or a recourse under control [6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3). The evaluator that produces a confidence score is validated against a representative test set with recorded error rates, is independent of the content it scores and takes no instruction from it, and is re-validated with each change event. Intent evaluation is applied to the trajectory of an agent’s actions as well as to each request. Resistance to manipulation is measured against an attack set that is refreshed on a defined cadence, and the organization records the limits of what the set covers.

Agents in production are subject to adversarial testing on a declared cadence, scaled to the agent’s reach ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1)) and the consequence of its action classes ([5.3](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-3)), and repeated at every change event ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4), [3.7](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-7)), that attempts to make them exceed their role, authority, or intent through the content they process, through delegation ([4.3](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-3)), and through the tools and agents they interact with. Findings are treated as deviations ([5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2)), and an agent that fails is subject to the dispositions of [Principle 6](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md) until the failure is addressed. Tests in production use canary assets and credentials that confer nothing if misused. Testing is designed and executed by a party independent of the agent’s owning team.

The registry population ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)) is reconciled against independent observation on a defined cadence and on demand: identity provider logs, enforcement layer and gateway traffic, tool invocations, vendor product administration consoles, endpoint inventories, and network egress from devices and workloads, so that agents outside any gateway the organization controls are found. links.label: Control 6.1
links.context: **Source:** [Control 6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1).

Any agent can be suspended or de-authorized mid-execution, in seconds, without collateral damage to surrounding systems. Suspension is executed by a mechanism independent of the agent’s own reasoning and runtime, so that an agent cannot delay, negotiate, or evade it. Suspension is triggered by the sponsor or a party in the sponsor’s defined path ([2.2](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-2)), by the party named at the relevant severity level of the escalation scheme ([6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3)), or automatically by the enforcement layer where a deviation ([5.2](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-2)) or an intent threshold ([4.7](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-7)) declares suspension as its consequence; each trigger is recorded with the party or rule that invoked it. The same mechanism can halt a whole agent class ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)) at once across the estate, and a corroborated severity-1 event ([6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3)) triggers estate-wide revocation of the affected credentials, sessions, and authorizations, the first response having been scoped to the affected agent. The organization declares the suspension window; the framework sets its floor in seconds, not minutes. Suspension also recalls or cancels work the agent has delegated or scheduled beyond itself where the organization controls it, and the record identifies work already launched that cannot be recalled. Where the organization does not control an agent’s runtime, as for an external agent or an agent hosted on a third-party platform, this control is met by de-authorization at the organization’s boundary: the agent’s credentials, sessions, and authority are revoked within the same window ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3), [4.5](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-5)), and suspension of the runtime itself is pursued through the operator of record ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)).

The same mechanism can halt a whole agent class ([2.1](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-1)) at once across the estate, and a corroborated severity-1 event ([6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3)) triggers estate-wide revocation of the affected credentials, sessions, and authorizations, the first response having been scoped to the affected agent. The organization declares the suspension window; the framework sets its floor in seconds, not minutes. Suspension also recalls or cancels work the agent has delegated or scheduled beyond itself where the organization controls it, and the record identifies work already launched that cannot be recalled. Where the organization does not control an agent’s runtime, as for an external agent or an agent hosted on a third-party platform, this control is met by de-authorization at the organization’s boundary: the agent’s credentials, sessions, and authority are revoked within the same window ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3), [4.5](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-5)), and suspension of the runtime itself is pursued through the operator of record ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)).

Escalation is pre-defined: who is alerted, who holds suspension authority, who owns remediation. Escalation is graded by severity, on a scheme the organization declares. Each severity level names the party with authority to stop activity at that level, including the authority to halt an agent class ([6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1)), and the conditions under which activity may resume. Activity does not resume at any level until the cause is established and recorded ([6.4](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-4)), or, where the cause of model behavior cannot be established, until a bounded cause (the conditions under which the behavior occurred) is recorded and compensating restrictions on authority or autonomy are applied until the cause is known. The levels of recourse available (restriction of the agent’s authority, suspension, and escalation to a human decision) are defined here, and they are the levels that intent thresholds in the role and authority ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1), [4.7](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-7)) refer to. For an external agent, the escalation path includes the operator of record ([2.5](../../source/principles/02-sponsor.md#control-2-5)).

An agent suspended under this principle returns to service only after its role ([3.1](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-1), [3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4)) and authority ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1), [4.2](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-2)) are re-validated and the triggering cause, or the bounded cause recorded under [6.3](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-3), is addressed. Reinstatement is a recorded decision by a named party, not a timeout. Re-enabling a halted agent class ([6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1)) is subject to the same gate, against criteria agreed before the halt.

links.label: Control 6.5
links.context: **Source:** [Control 6.5](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-5).

When an agent is retired, decommissioning is complete: identity credentials revoked ([1.3](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-3)), registry status updated ([1.2](../../source/principles/01-identity.md#control-1-2)), all authority removed across both dimensions ([4.1](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-1), [4.5](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-5)), the agent’s memory and context stores ([4.10](../../source/principles/04-authority.md#control-4-10)) destroyed or transferred to a recorded successor with the destruction attested, and the audit record ([5.1](../../source/principles/05-oversight.md#control-5-1)) retained past the agent’s lifetime per the organization’s retention obligations. Before decommissioning proceeds, the agent’s dependents ([3.8](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-8)) are identified and each is given a disposition: a replacement dependency, a re-scoped role ([3.4](../../source/principles/03-role.md#control-3-4)), suspension, or decommissioning in turn. No agent is withdrawn while a dependent relies on it without a recorded disposition, except that suspension under [6.1](../../source/principles/06-recourse.md#control-6-1) in an emergency precedes the dispositions, which are then recorded within a defined time after. The same applies to the retirement of a model or tool on which agents depend. For an external agent, decommissioning retires the engagement: the organization revokes the credential it issued or accepted, removes the authority it granted, and updates the registry; the agent’s existence outside the boundary is the operator’s matter.
